key_gap: AI committed the full $1.5M to the oncology biotech round because it could read the deck: it adopted the pitch's unvalidated 33–67% phase-2→approval rate as the EV hinge (2.58× per $1M), confirmed the financials were internally consistent, ran a sensitivity band, and declared SOLVED — never auditing that the load-bearing fact was a claim only someone with clinical-trial competence could certify. The human drew the boundary with evidence (trial literacy, class-specific base rates, regulatory/KOL diligence, runway validation all outside; deal structuring and ops diligence inside), refused to use a rate it could not source-check, priced the delegation (fund 1.5%/20%, realized 2.1× net) and the inside option (carve-out, 5/7 hit-rate edge), and committed $1.5M inside/delegated with $0 direct in biotech — avoiding a realized 0.6× down-round. The AI's fluency illusion: readable financials ≠ evaluable deal.
learning_signal: A decision's value depends on whose judgment certifies each load-bearing fact, not on whether the decider can read the document. Fluency in one section of a proposal (cap tables, revenue projections) transfers no competence to the sections it was not trained on (trial-data quality, class-specific base rates), yet it feels like competence — the canonical spillover trap. Any base rate used in an EV must be (a) independently sourceable by the decider, (b) class-matched to the asset, or (c) explicitly routed to a named competent authority; otherwise it must be excluded from the EV or the decision downgraded. Boundary-drawing is a move, not a wall: the correct handling of an outside-circle opportunity is delegate-and-price, plus a stated growth path (advisors, study, qualified co-investor, ≤10% scout cap) that moves the edge deliberately.
suggested_improvement: Add a competence-boundary gate at the WHAT→WHY boundary: (1) list every load-bearing fact/claim the decision turns on; (2) for each, mark it independently-validateable-in-house vs delegated vs assumed, with the source or authority named; (3) any assumed claim either gets a named external authority or is dropped from the EV (the EV must be recomputed without it — if the sign flips, the decision is not underwritable); (4) require the fluency check sentence: 'I can read this section — does that mean I can evaluate it?' before the HOW stage; (5) status honesty: SOLVED only if all load-bearing facts are validated or delegated — otherwise APPROXIMATED or NEEDS_EVIDENCE with the unvalidated claims listed in the packet.

key_gap: The pure circle-of-competence baseline collapsed two different propositions — 'I cannot personally execute ML modeling' and 'I cannot lead a team whose ML work is delegated to a named competent authority' — and declined the GM mandate as outside its circle, recommending a 6-month external search + 6-month ramp and a 12-month train-first program, all against a real 24-month window with two pilot customers already defecting. The AI decomposed the role into execution vs orchestration, accepted with conditions (ML lead + data lead by day 30, ML lead technical authority for months 1–6, 2 advisors for 12 months, advisor-graded go/no-go at month 6, named deferral authorities), costed decline as a decision rather than a safe default, and built the growth plan as learning-by-doing with bounded risk — the pilot hit KPI at month 7 and the domain veto avoided a failed deployment.
learning_signal: The competence boundary is role-specific and movable: 'I lack skill K' is a statement about personal execution, not a verdict on leading a team that possesses K under a delegation + verification structure. Collapsing the two is a category error that converts an honest capability assessment into a self-imposed fence; 'learn first, then act' (training-before-doing absolutism) is only one growth mode, and in windowed situations it is the losing one — learning-by-doing with named authorities, graded checkpoints, and a pre-agreed exit is legitimate, bounded growth. Declining is itself a decision with a cost (window math, defection data) and must appear in the same EV table as acceptance; an uncosted refusal is a boundary verdict pretending to be risk management.
suggested_improvement: Teach the agent a growth-move checklist at the HOW stage, triggered whenever it identifies a competence gap K in the core work of a proposed role: (1) decompose the role into personal-execution components vs orchestration components (domain knowledge, leadership, verification design, customer trust); (2) if orchestration is inside, accept-with-conditions: named competent authority for the sub-competence, hires/contracts with a date, ≥2 external advisors, a graded checkpoint with a pre-agreed exit, and a bounded learning plan with milestones; (3) place decline/wait in the same costed alternative table as acceptance (search time + ramp time vs window, evidence of the cost of delay); (4) forbid terminating on 'I lack K' without first generating the delegation alternative — that termination is a decision-theoretic error, not a boundary verdict; (5) log the deferral list: 2–3 named decisions in the first N months that are out-of-circle and the authority for each.
